lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Isn't that Heracles? It is — by Heracles, it's nobody else. The bow, the club, the lion-skin, the size — that's the whole Heracles. So he's dead, then? The son of Zeus? Tell me, glorious conqueror — you're a corpse? Because I used to sacrifice to you up there. As to a god.
lines.description: dry recognition turning to surgical skepticism; amused, not impressed

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: And quite right you were. The actual Heracles is in heaven keeping company with the gods, and he's got Hebe of the lovely ankles. I'm his shade.
lines.description: dignified correction, trying to preserve grandeur under absurd terms

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I'm sorry — his what? The god's shade? Is it actually possible to be half a god and half dead?
lines.description: flat incredulity; pounces on the contradiction with relish

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Yes. Because he hasn't died. I have. I'm the image of him.
lines.description: stiff, over-clear explanation; already irritated

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Ah. I see. He handed you over to Pluto as a substitute for himself, and now you get to be the corpse in his place.
lines.description: deadpan deduction, calmly making it worse

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Something like that.
lines.description: reluctant concession, clipped and uncomfortable

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Then how, given that Aeacus is so meticulous, did he fail to spot that you weren't him? How did he accept a counterfeit Heracles right there at the gate?
lines.description: legalistic cross-examination; crisp, needling precision

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Because I was an exact likeness.
lines.description: defensive, simple answer as if that should settle it

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: True enough. So exact, in fact, that you might actually be him. Consider the possibility, then, that it's the other way round — you're Heracles, and the shade is the one who married Hebe upstairs.
lines.description: smooth trap-springing logic; mild tone, devastating implication

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You've got some nerve, and a mouth on you. Keep mocking me and you'll find out very shortly what kind of god I'm the shade of.
lines.description: threatening, pride wounded; big heroic bluster cracking

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: [chuckles] The bow's already unsheathed, I see, arrow ready. But what have I got to be afraid of? I've died once already. Tell me, though — by your precious Heracles — when he was alive, were you with him then too, being his shade? Or were the two of you one person during life, and only after death did you split up — he flew off to the gods, and you, the shade, came down here, which is what shades are supposed to do?
lines.description: chuckling contempt, fearless; accelerates into relentless questioning

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: One really shouldn't even respond to a man who's heckling like this. But fine — listen. Whatever there was of Amphitryon in Heracles, that part has died, and that's all of me. Whatever was Zeus's is up in heaven with the gods.
lines.description: forced patience, formal theology deployed through gritted teeth

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Now I understand perfectly. Alcmene, you're saying, gave birth to two Heracleses at the same time — one by Amphitryon, one by Zeus. So all this time the two of you were twins by the same mother and nobody noticed.
lines.description: mock enlightenment; perfectly reasonable tone makes it ridiculous

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: No, you idiot. We were both the same man.
lines.description: snaps, exasperated and losing dignity

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: It's not easy to grasp, you understand — two Heracleses compounded into one. Unless the two of you were a sort of hippocentaur arrangement, a man and a god fused together into a single creature.
lines.description: blandly helpful, piling absurd imagery with scholarly calm

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Well, don't you think everyone's put together that way — from two things, soul and body? So what's to prevent the soul, which came from Zeus, from being in heaven, while I — the mortal part — am here among the dead?
lines.description: rhetorical recovery attempt; earnest, a little too eager

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Yes, but my dear son of Amphitryon — that would be a fine argument if you were a body. As it is, you're a bodiless shade. So you're now in danger of producing three Heracleses.
lines.description: kindly address, then deadpan demolition; savor the final count

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: Three how?
lines.description: caught off guard; small, wary, genuinely confused

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Like this. If one of you is in heaven, and you — the shade — are down here with us, and the body got dissolved and turned into dust long ago, that makes three. [pause] And you'll need to come up with a third father for the body, too. Have a think about who.
lines.description: patient arithmetic, then delayed knife-twist after the pause

lines.speaker: Heracles
lines.text: You've got nerve, and you're a sophist. Who are you anyway?
lines.description: angry but cornered; bluster giving way to suspicion

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: The shade of Diogenes of Sinope. The man himself — no, by Zeus, not 'with the immortal gods' — he's keeping company with the best of the dead, and he's laughing at Homer and all this frigid drivel.
lines.description: proudly dry self-introduction; final contempt lands cleanly
